own_scenes.desc: El silencio en el corazón de 1966 es el de la explosión nuclear. Los adolescentes fueron la primera generación criada con la bomba atómica y de hidrógeno; según Jeff Nuttall (Bomb Culture), quienes no habían llegado a la pubertad en 1945 «nunca conocieron un sentido de futuro». Las aritméticas del momento (veintiún años entre las dos guerras mundiales, 1945 + 21 = 1966) y las crisis de Berlín (1961) y de los misiles de Cuba (1962) convencieron a muchos de que no llegarían al final de la década: si no hay futuro, todo es AHORA. Las primeras canciones atómicas eran triunfalistas; «Old Man Atom» de Sam Hinton (1950) fue prohibida y «We’ll All Go Together When We Go» de Tom Lehrer fue la excepción satírica. The War Game, de Peter Watkins (encargada por la BBC y prohibida por presión del gobierno laborista de Wilson en 1965), muestra un ataque nuclear sobre Kent con estética de noticiario: el silencio del destello, ojos derretidos, soldados rematando a los moribundos. Se estrenó con calificación X en marzo de 1966 y circuló como un samizdat. Cuatro días antes de que saliera «A Quiet Explosion», un B-52 perdió cuatro bombas H sobre Palomares (17 de enero de 1966).

refs.q: So this is the lacuna at the heart of this extraordinary year: the sound of nuclear explosion.
refs.para: So this is the lacuna at the heart of this extraordinary year: the sound of nuclear explosion. For the previous twenty-one years, ever since the hecatombs of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, it had invaded the consciousness of the world. The effects were fundamental and, as yet, ill understood, but they poisoned everything. Even so, there were those who continued to think in the old way: the Cold War, the arms race, Mutually Assured Destruction. They were in charge of the weapons, and they clung to the certainties of 1945.
refs.chapter: Enero: A Quiet Explosion: la CND, la protesta y la conspiración del silencio

refs.q: They were the first generation in history to have grown up in this insane world of A- and H-bombs.
refs.para: They were the first generation in history to have grown up in this insane world of A- and H-bombs. They had had to face a potentially blasted future from the very beginning. Pop was their culture, and the huge amounts of money flowing into the music industry engendered a confidence that propelled many ever further and deeper, as they began to explore this and other fears. From 1965 on, pop culture offered, as the pioneering critic Paul Williams observed, ‘a huge new playground to create and communicate and be perverse in’.
refs.chapter: Enero: A Quiet Explosion: la CND, la protesta y la conspiración del silencio

refs.q: The War Game lasts for only forty-seven minutes but seems to go on for days.
refs.para: The War Game lasts for only forty-seven minutes but seems to go on for days. It remains a profoundly disturbing experience, indelibly etched on the sixties teenagers who saw it in art houses or in cinema clubs, who watched their certainties explode on the screen as quickly as nitrate film. The action builds slowly, from international tension – such as existed in Europe at that time – to the use of nuclear weapons. As soon as this occurs, the unthinkable and the barely imaginable is visualised on screen.
refs.chapter: Enero: A Quiet Explosion: la CND, la protesta y la conspiración del silencio

refs.q: The War Game quickly fell victim to the very thing it was designed to oppose: the conspiracy of silence.
refs.para: The War Game quickly fell victim to the very thing it was designed to oppose: the conspiracy of silence. Subsequent research has revealed that, right from the very beginning, the film aroused anxiety among the BBC top brass: Head of Music and Documentary Programmes Huw Wheldon, BBC Director General Sir Hugh Carleton-Greene, and Lord Normanbrook, the chairman of the BBC Board of Governors. They quickly took soundings from the Home Office.
refs.chapter: Enero: A Quiet Explosion: la CND, la protesta y la conspiración del silencio

refs.q: On 17 January 1966, a B-52 bomber collided with a Boeing KC-135 Stratotanker off the coast of Spain
refs.para: Four days before the record was released, the US suffered its most serious nuclear accident to date. On 17 January 1966, a B-52 bomber collided with a Boeing KC-135 Stratotanker off the coast of Spain, killing seven crew members in the two planes. The bomber was carrying four hydrogen bombs, three of which crashed to earth near Palomares, on the southern coast of Spain. The non-nuclear explosives detonated, spreading plutonium and uranium over several acres.
refs.chapter: Enero: A Quiet Explosion: la CND, la protesta y la conspiración del silencio
